about: Verified evidence base behind PhysTutorBench v2 (methodology.html). Produced by an automated deep-research harness: 5 search angles -> 28 fetched sources -> 138 extracted claims -> 3-vote adversarial verification of the 25 highest-value claims. 22 confirmed (>=2/3 votes). Final synthesis was authored by a human from this corpus. 3 ICAP claims could not finish verification before a provider rate limit and are treated as canonical in the write-up.

round1.note: PER/tutoring/validity backbone; auto-synthesis + ICAP votes cut off by rate limit

round2.note: LLM-side gaps; full synthesis; pinned judge-bias, prior-benchmark, ICAP citations

confirmed_claims.claim: Across 62 intro physics courses (N=6542), interactive-engagement courses averaged normalized gain <g>=0.48 (sd .14) vs 0.23 (sd .04) for traditional, ~2x more effective.
Normalized gain g = (post% - pre%)/(100 - pre%): actual gain over maximum possible gain.
The FCI (Hestenes, Wells & Swackhamer 1992, The Physics Teacher 30(3):141-158) is a validated instrument for students' force/motion conceptions.
The FCI measures conceptual understanding and alternative conceptions (misconceptions) about force/motion; a diagnostic suitable for sourcing validated misconceptions.

Authorship correction: PRPER 16,010108 (2020) is Coletta & Steinert, a rebuttal defending normalized gain; the Nissen et al. normalized-gain-vs-Cohen's-d paper is PRPER 14,010115 (2018, arXiv:1612.09180).
Coletta & Steinert (2020): the prescore bias attributed to normalized gain by Nissen does not exist under careful analysis; the apparent bias is omitted-variable bias in the competing analysis.
Coletta & Steinert (2020): Cohen's d is less informative than normalized gain as a single-parameter effectiveness measure; recommend continuing to use normalized gain.
FCI item Q.29 (atmospheric pressure) shows reduced correct-answer rates pre->post in some classes: instruction made performance worse on this item.
Many students answer an FCI item correctly without the intended concept, and many who learned it still miss it: item correctness is a poor proxy for the targeted concept.
Post-instruction learners had a worse correct-response rate on Q.29, making the item less discriminating of ability.
Item Response Theory predicts observed FCI gains/losses fairly well, offering a model-based alternative to raw answer-change proportions.
Because responses are non-deterministic, up to ~25% of answers can change on retest with NO learning: pre/post change is partly measurement noise.
In a no-learning test-retest, apparent gains/losses can range 0%-100%, so raw gain figures alone cannot be read as evidence of learning.
Individual normalized FCI gain g correlates positively & significantly with pre-instruction FCI score in 3/4 IE populations (r=0.15-0.33): g is not independent of incoming level.
Across 38 IE classes (2948 students), class-average normalized FCI gain correlates with class-average pre-score (r=0.63, p<0.0001): g is not population-independent across groups.

Normalized FCI gain g correlates with scientific-reasoning ability (Lawson) at r=0.51 (p<0.0001, n=65), stronger than with prescore: reasoning ability is a hidden confound of g as an efficacy measure.
VanLehn (2011): human tutoring vs no-tutoring effect size d=0.79, far below the cited 'two-sigma' (d=2.0).
VanLehn (2011): intelligent tutoring systems reach d=0.76, nearly equal to human tutoring (0.79): automated tutors can match humans on learning outcomes.
VanLehn (2011): the belief that finer interaction granularity necessarily increases effectiveness was NOT confirmed; assumed-good design features must be validated against learning, not presumed.
Chi et al. (2001) framed tutoring effectiveness as three competing hypotheses (tutor-centered, student-centered, interactive) a benchmark must distinguish among.

Chi et al. (2001): students learned just as effectively when tutors were experimentally suppressed from giving explanations/feedback, falsifying that tutor explanation delivery is the primary driver of learning.

Chi et al. (2001): interactive-tutoring learning is attributed to deeper/more scaffolding episodes plus students taking control (reading more): construct of good tutoring = eliciting student construction, not disclosure.

round2_gap_fill_confirmed_claims.claim: LLM-judge validation standard = agreement with human experts; strong judges (GPT-4) reach >80% agreement on non-tie votes (matching human-human), dropping to ~60-66% with ties.
LLM judges show documented position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases plus limited reasoning.
round2_gap_fill_confirmed_claims.source: arXiv:2306.05685; arXiv:2410.02736 (Ye et al., CALM, ICLR 2025)

round2_gap_fill_confirmed_claims.claim: CALM quantifies 12 distinct LLM-judge biases; position-bias robustness rate falls below 0.5 with 3-4 candidates, so judges are not reliable by default.
Self-preference/self-enhancement is a measurable bias (GPT-4 significant); mechanism contested (self-recognition vs perplexity/familiarity).
round2_gap_fill_confirmed_claims.source: arXiv:2404.13076 (Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024); arXiv:2410.21819 (Wataoka et al., workshop)

round2_gap_fill_confirmed_claims.claim: MathDial: ~3k teacher-LLM-student tutoring dialogues w/ teacher-move taxonomy; process-only, LLM-simulated students, no learning-outcome criterion (2025 follow-up: simulated results inflated).
CIMA: tutoring dialogue dataset; next-tutor-utterance generation scored by BLEU/BERTScore; process proxy only, no learning gain.
AI Teacher Test: comparative human judgment of pedagogical ability; both LLMs scored worse than human teachers, esp. on helpfulness (fluency != pedagogy); no learning criterion.
TSCC: freely-available one-to-one tutoring dialogue corpus w/ SETT annotation; process/dialogue only, no learning-gain metric.
Bridge: 700 real tutoring conversations w/ expert remediation decisions; evaluated by human preference; authors list learning impact as future work (process/quality only).
MathTutorBench (SOTA): scores open-ended pedagogical quality with a trained reward model (expert-vs-novice ~0.84); no real student learning-outcome criterion.
ICAP (Chi & Wylie 2014): ordering Passive<Active<Constructive<Interactive, operationalized via overt behaviors; ordering/operationalization empirically contested.

round2_open_unverified: Data contamination/leakage primary source (gap #4): not among confirmed claims; treat as open.
Tutor CoPilot RCT outcomes/population (gap #5; EdWorkingPaper ai24-1054 / arXiv:2410.03017): not independently verified.
caveat: Some automated search hits returned implausible identifiers (e.g., future-dated arXiv IDs); these were excluded from the write-up in favor of the canonical record. Confirm every citation against its source of record before formal use.

v3_prospectus_run.about: Evidence layer behind concept-paper.html. Produced by a multi-agent harness: 6 deep-research sweeps + 6 adversarial expert-reviewer critiques (run concurrently) -> primary-source verification of load-bearing claims -> funding-panel synthesis. 17 agents total. Resolves the two open gaps flagged in round 2 (inventory-contamination primary source; Tutor CoPilot outcomes) and adds the adjacent-AI-tutor-learning-gain literature, the measurement-science deepening, the automated-evaluation-validity literature, and the funding landscape. Every citation below was checked against an actually-fetched source; re-confirm before formal submission.

load_bearing_verified.claim: Real-learning RCTs of LLM tutors now EXIST but NONE computes a cheap automated transcript-quality score and shows it predicts that same student's measured real learning gain (the B1 link). The defensible novelty is the LINK, not the endpoint.
sources: Wang et al. Tutor CoPilot arXiv:2410.03017 (+4 p.p.)

load_bearing_verified.claim: A Gates-Foundation-backed funder (Digital Promise 'EDU AI', up to ~$8M) frames the exact construct PhysTutorBench measures in funder-authored language (answers too quickly; talk too much; Helpful Assistant Bias gives away answers vs supporting productive struggle). K-12 math; construct transfers to physics.

Both obvious federal homes (NSF, IES) face acute 2025-26 disruption, BUT the specific '$7.0B/-23%/EDU-folded' NSF figure was a PROPOSED House bill, NOT enacted; a CR funded NSF at ~$9.1B (FY2025 level) with EDU preserved. The IES cuts (~$881M contracts, 100+ staff) ARE verified.

resolved_open_gaps.tutor_copilot_outcomes: VERIFIED: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb & Demszky; arXiv:2410.03017 / DOI 10.26300/81nh-8262 (EdWorkingPaper ai24-1054). Tutors (not students) randomized; primary outcome = exit-ticket mastery (+4 p.p., p<0.01; +9 p.p. for lowest-rated tutors); 550k-message pedagogy classifier is condition-level/descriptive, NOT bridged to individual gain. N differs by version (900/1,800 arXiv v2; >700/1,000 Nov-2025 working paper) -- cite per version. EdWorkingPaper number internally inconsistent (24-1054 vs 24-1056); prefer arXiv ID + DOI.

key_corrections_for_writeup: Novelty: scope to the missing LINK (automated metric -> same student's real gain), not the missing endpoint; cite Kestin/Tutor CoPilot as feasibility + motivation, not competitors.

ITS canon: concede Cognitive Tutors / knowledge tracing / VanLehn d=0.76 already bridged hand-built cognitive models to learning; increment = validating the cognitive-model-free, bias-prone LLM-as-judge/reward-model evaluator. Delete 'invalidate the entire paradigm'.
Gate G1: disattenuated, CI-based, cross-validated (not a single point r>=0.5), or a null is an attenuation artifact.
Primary outcome: covariate-adjusted IRT/Rasch latent change, not raw normalized gain; do NOT assume scoreable FCI cluster subscales (contested dimensionality).
Citation hygiene: LearnLM '+5.5 p.p.' belongs to the Eedi study, NOT arXiv:2412.16429 (which is +31% expert preference); FY2026 NSF cut is proposed-not-enacted.
